name: Roman Republic
summary: The Roman state before the emperors, governed by elected magistrates and the Senate. It conquered the Mediterranean before collapsing into civil wars.

location.value: Rome and Italy, expanding to rule the whole Mediterranean by the 1st century BCE.

terrain.value: The Italian peninsula, the Apennines, and the Tiber river.

resources.value: Italian farmland, and later the tribute and grain of conquered provinces (Sicily, Africa, Egypt).

disasters.value: Not specifically documented in the sources checked.

population.value: Not in the Wikipedia infobox. Censuses counted adult male citizens (about 900,000 in 70 BCE).

urbanisation.value: Rome grew into the largest city of the Mediterranean.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Roman and Latin colonies spread across Italy. Huge numbers of captives were brought to Italy as slaves.

economicBase.value: Agriculture by smallholders, then large slave-worked estates (latifundia), plus war plunder and provincial taxes.

tradeRoutes.value: Mediterranean sea trade after defeating Carthage.

wealth.value: No estimate is given in the sources checked. Carthage paid indemnities of 2,200 talents (241 BCE) and 10,000 talents (201 BCE).

moneyAndTax.value: The silver denarius (from about 211 BCE). Wartime loans and provincial tribute.

inequality.value: Patricians and a wealthy nobility above plebeians, with mass slavery. Debt and land disputes drove political conflict.

governmentType.value: A consular republic: two consuls elected each year, the Senate and the popular assemblies. An elective oligarchy.

keyRulers.value: Lucius Junius Brutus (first consul, 509 BCE). Scipio Africanus. The Gracchi. Marius. Sulla (dictator 82 BCE). Julius Caesar (dictator for life 44 BCE). Octavian.

succession.value: Annual elections. Two consuls with mutual veto, and tribunes of the plebs with veto power.

institutions.value: The Senate, consuls, tribunes and assemblies. The Twelve Tables (law code), and the Lex Hortensia (287 BCE) making plebeian laws binding on all.

stability.value: The Conflict of the Orders. Three Servile (slave) Wars. The Social War (91–87 BCE). Civil wars (Marius versus Sulla, Caesar versus Pompey).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between populares and optimates. Generals with private armies. Caesar’s assassination (15 March 44 BCE).

armyAndTech.value: Citizen legions, reformed into professional armies (associated with Marius), and a navy built for the Punic Wars (the corvus boarding bridge).

majorWars.value: Conquest of Italy. The Punic Wars against Carthage (264–146 BCE). The Macedonian Wars. Caesar’s Gallic Wars. Civil wars ending at Actium (31 BCE).

territoryChange.value: From about 10,000 km² (326 BCE) to 1.95 million km² (50 BCE) (Wikipedia infobox).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Etruscans, Samnites, Carthage, Macedon, the Seleucids and Pontus. Italian allies (socii).

inventions.value: Roads (the Via Appia, 312 BCE), aqueducts (Aqua Appia), and early use of concrete.

openness.value: Absorbed Etruscan and Greek culture and Italian allies.

artsArchitecture.value: Temples and forums. Plautus’ comedies. Cicero’s speeches. Realistic portrait busts.

socialStructure.value: Patricians, plebeians, equestrians, freedmen and slaves. Slavery fuelled revolts (e.g. Spartacus, 73–71 BCE).

sharedIdentity.value: Roman citizenship and “SPQR” (the Senate and People of Rome). Hostility to kings.

neighbours.value: Etruscans, Samnites, Gauls, Greek cities, Carthage, Macedon and the Seleucid Empire.

ideasReligions.value: Adopted Greek art, philosophy and gods. Spread Latin across the West.

colonisation.value: Founded colonies across Italy and conquered provinces around the Mediterranean.

riseSignals.value: A disciplined army, a network of Italian allies, naval innovation, and victory over Carthage and the Hellenistic kingdoms.

peakPeriod.value: The 2nd century BCE, as master of the Mediterranean.

declineSignals.value: Mass slavery, land inequality, political violence, and generals with personal armies, all breaking down the republican system.

outcome.value: Transformation into monarchy. After Actium (31 BCE), Octavian became Augustus (27 BCE), and the Roman Empire replaced the Republic.

sources.value: Roman historians (Livy, Polybius, Plutarch), Cicero’s writings, inscriptions and coins. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Beard (2015).

overallCertainty.value: Good for the late Republic. Early history (founding, 509 BCE, the sack of Rome in 390/387 BCE) mixes legend and fact.
